title: Silence
hookLine: silence makes room for God to speak
tomorrow: Mia's right there. so why does Sofia keep checking her phone?

cards: Then nothing, not even the dots. Silence after something hard can feel like a verdict, and a thumb hovers over the keyboard to fill it. Should she text again?
Inside the Church, silence has two schools of thought, and both of them have a case. One says keep it. The other says speak up and sing.
It's a question for prayer too: when to talk, and when to wait.

teach.h: NOT IN THE WIND OR THE FIRE.
teach.b: The first side says: keep the silence, because that's where God speaks. Elijah, worn out and hiding on the mountain of God, watches a great wind, then an earthquake, then fire, and the Lord is in none of them.
Then, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "a whistling of a gentle air." That's when he covers his face and steps out to listen.
The Church's instructions for Mass ask for sacred silence at set moments, such as after the readings and after Communion. On this side, silence isn't empty. It's room.
Some Catholics love a quiet weekday Mass for exactly this. The second side says: speak up, sing out. The Church's prayer is public, spoken and sung.

The Second Vatican Council asked the people at Mass to take part with acclamations, responses, psalms and songs, not to sit there as silent spectators. A faith that never says anything can shrink into something private.
Some Catholics love a full choir and a loud Gloria for exactly that. Here's the turn: both views come from the same paragraph.
The Council lists the singing and the speaking, and then adds that at the proper times all should keep a reverent silence.
Ecclesiastes put it in one line long before: "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak."
The argument among Catholics isn't silence against speech. It's which time is now.

how: At Mass the Church asks for moments of sacred silence, such as after the readings and after Communion, alongside sung and spoken responses; Catholics also keep quiet time in prayer or before the Blessed Sacrament.

games.q: your friend says a quiet Mass with no music feels empty and cold. you love singing too. what's the strongest case for the quiet side?
o: Elijah met the Lord in a gentle air, after the noise passed.
quiet Masses are the older, more correct way to pray.
music at Mass is a distraction the Church only puts up with.
games.why: the quiet side has Elijah: not in the wind or the fire, but in the gentle air. the singing side has the Council: no silent spectators. the same paragraph asks for both.

practice: Let the next stretch be silence: nothing playing, nothing to read. Listen for the quietest sound in the room, a fan, a clock, your own breathing, and stay with it.
If the noise in your head gets loud, let it pass like Elijah's wind. If you pray, you can say Samuel's line once, speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth, and then simply listen.

wordCard.voice: Silence. Quiet kept on purpose, at the right time, so there's room for someone else to speak.

orig.note: Latin, 3 Kings 19:12 in the Vulgate: a whistling of a gentle air, where Elijah heard the Lord.

carryVoice: Your line: room to speak. Elijah heard it only after the wind, the earthquake and the fire had passed. Go quietly.
